meta.subtitle: 530 expressions · 111 everyday, 234 particle verbs, 94 idioms, 91 proverbs · both directions
meta.desc: 530 Danish set phrases, particle verbs, idioms and proverbs, in four subdecks: 111 everyday phrases, 234 particle verbs, 94 idioms and 91 proverbs. Both study directions come as two cards of one expression — Danish → English (see the Danish, recall the meaning) and English → Danish (see an English meaning, recall the Danish) — each with a schedule of its own. This is a companion to the five level decks, Danish A1 to C1, and not one of them: a level is a list of words, and an expression is a unit a list of words cannot see. Nothing here is taught by any of the five, so the two can be studied together without repeating an entry. The PHRASES are the expressions Wiktionary files as phrases and does not mark as idiomatic — mostly the everyday formulas a Danish speaker uses as one piece (det her, den her, om det …). The PARTICLE VERBS are a verb and a particle or a preposition that together mean something the verb alone does not (have brug for, kunne lide, holde op …) — Danish is built on them, the particle carries the stress, and the card shows the present, past and perfect of the whole where Wiktionary gives them. The IDIOMS are expressions whose meaning is not their words' (gøre en myg til en elefant, bide i det sure æble, aldrig i livet …), and the PROVERBS the sayings Wiktionary files as proverbs (tid er penge, væggene har ører, intet nyt under solen …). Within each subdeck the expressions come in the order of how many of Tatoeba's Danish sentences contain them, a particle verb being counted with its verb in any form; 206 of the 530 are found there, and the rest follow in the order of how common their words are in film and television subtitles. The particle verbs and idioms are the commonest of the many Wiktionary lists, chosen by that same order. Real example sentences come with 203 of the 530 expressions, three apiece for 111, with the expression picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Expressions, meanings, forms and the idiom and proverb labels: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Order: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR, then a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba, CC BY 2.0 FR.
